Serbian FBReporter: German massacre in Kragujevac, mass murder of Serbian school children

content.p: On 21 October 1941, in and around the central Serbian town of Kragujevac, German soldiers shot thousands of men and boys who had been rounded up, some of them taken from their classrooms. They were hostages, chosen not for anything they had done but to fill a quota. The German army's rule in occupied Serbia that autumn was that 100 civilians would die for every German soldier killed and 50 for every one wounded. Kragujevac was one place where it was applied.

The exact number of dead is still given in different ways. The commander who ordered the shooting reported 2,300 hostages killed at Kragujevac. Later accounts speak of more than 2,800 or about 3,000. Among the dead were pupils of the town's secondary school and some of their teachers, and their story became the one most often told about the day, in a poem, in two films and in a monument that is now the town's emblem.

The Spomenik Database, a project documenting Yugoslav war memorials, dates the origin of the rule to 16 September 1941, when Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel issued a directive authorising retaliatory killings of civilians for deaths among German soldiers caused by partisan fighters. The directive allowed up to 100 executions for each German killed. Nenad Đorđević of the Kragujevac Memorial Park gave the ratio to CGTN as 100 Serbs for each dead German and 50 for each wounded one.

The records of the postwar Hostages Trial show how the rule travelled down the chain of command. According to the trial's law report, General Franz Böhme was given charge of military affairs in Serbia after Hitler signed an order on 16 September, and the whole executive power in the country passed to him. The report says he issued orders on 25 September and 10 October 1941 to the units under his command. The prosecution at Nuremberg later read out German reports that cited the "order dated 10 October 41", and pointed out that its code number referred back to the Keitel directive of 16 September. In one of those reports, a single German soldier killed and two lightly wounded produced a demand for 200 hostages: 100 times one, and 50 times two.

That is the bureaucratic background. The immediate cause, in the Spomenik Database's account, was an attack by partisans on a group of soldiers of the 920th Landesschützen Battalion, who were stationed in a schoolhouse near Gornji Milanovac, less than 40 kilometres west of Kragujevac, on 28 September. Ten German soldiers were killed. The database says Böhme, angry and worried about an uprising he could not control, ordered the arrest of thousands of men in Kragujevac and the surrounding region. World War II Day by Day describes the massacre as a reprisal for German losses in battles with communist partisans and with the Serbian nationalist Chetniks in the area.

The sources do not agree on the dates of the roundup or the shooting. A Serbian news site says the whole city was raided in the early morning of 19 October and that around 10,000 civilians aged 16 to 60 were arrested, among them a whole generation of high-school pupils taken straight from their classes. World War II Day by Day gives the same age range and the same figure of around 10,000 arrested, with German troops and collaborationist militia members doing the arresting, and says the nearly 3,000 victims were selected from among them. The Spomenik Database says those targeted were fighting-age males, mainly Jews, accused communists and suspected resisters, but that students, monks and priests were also taken, while men with valuable trades were reportedly spared.

Leon Lukman, who was ten at the time, told CGTN he heard gunshots while playing near his school and thought it was an exercise. According to CGTN, German soldiers entered classrooms on the day before the massacre and picked out teachers and pupils. The broadcaster reports that sixteen teachers and 60 children were killed at that school. The Spomenik Database puts the number of schoolboys killed, aged 12 to 15, at around 140 to 300, together with their teachers. The two figures cannot be reconciled from these pages; they may count different groups of pupils.

There is also the story of the headmaster. An inscription in the memorial park, as described by the Spomenik Database, alludes to the account that the school's principal, Miloje Pavlović, had been given permission by the Germans to leave but refused to step aside and said that if the children died he would die with them. CGTN records a teacher's last words as "Shoot! I am still teaching". Both are stories told about the day; the pages reviewed give no court record for either.

The Spomenik Database says most of the executions took place on the morning of 21 October at a cemetery area called Šumarice, just west of the town centre, over roughly seven hours, with groups of 50 to 100 people lined up in front of long pits. A Serbian news site says the shootings began at 6 p.m. on the day after the roundup, in groups of 400, and carried on into the next day at a lesser pace, and that the prisoners who were left were not released but kept as hostages for further reprisals. World War II Day by Day also says people were shot in groups of 400.

A telegram quoted in the same sources gives the German military commander's own explanation for choosing Kragujevac: "The executions in Kragujevac occurred although there had been no attacks on members of the Wehrmacht in this city, for the reason that not enough hostages could be found elsewhere." In other words, the town was picked because its men were available.

The Spomenik Database adds two further details. It says that after the shooting a military parade was held through the town centre, and that five days later the Germans picked 200 townspeople to bury the bodies, a job that took several days. It also says Böhme forbade anyone in the town to mark or commemorate the graves. The bodies lay in more than 30 mass graves, according to the same source.

Böhme's own accounting survives. In a report of 31 October 1941 to General Walter Kuntze, quoted in the Hostages Trial law report, he listed shootings of 405 hostages in Belgrade (4,750 there so far), 90 communists in the Šabac camp, 2,300 hostages in Kragujevac and 1,700 in Kraljevo. The prosecutor at Nuremberg read the same figures from a German report of 30 October on the numbers in the camp at Šabac.

Three kinds of number circulate. The contemporary German figure is 2,300. CGTN's 2025 report speaks of more than 2,800 civilians executed and of 300 children. World War II Day by Day says about 3,000, and the Serbian news site says more than 5,000, which is the highest figure among the pages reviewed and is given without a stated basis. None of these pages explains how its figure was reached. This account uses the German report's figure as the contemporary one and treats the rest as estimates.
CGTN adds a wider count, citing German records: at least 40,000 civilians in occupied Serbia killed by the regular army under the same rule. The records themselves were not examined here.

The man who gave the orders did not stand trial for them. According to the Spomenik Database, Böhme was captured trying to flee to Norway, was charged on 10 May 1947 and was due to be tried at Nuremberg with the Kragujevac massacre as the main charge, but killed himself by jumping from the fourth-floor window of the prison. The law report on the trial confirms that he died by suicide before the defendants were arraigned and that the tribunal ordered his name struck from the indictment.

The trial went ahead without him as the Hostages Trial, in which former senior German army officers, among them Wilhelm List, Maximilian von Weichs, Lothar Rendulic and Walter Kuntze, were charged over reprisal killings and destruction in occupied Greece, Yugoslavia, Albania and Norway. The tribunal sat from 8 July 1947 to 19 February 1948. The law report records that the evidence included Böhme's reports, including one to List in which he described the shooting of about 2,000 communists and Jews in reprisal for 22 men killed from a signals battalion. The verdicts on the surviving defendants are not covered by the pages reviewed here.

Desanka Maksimović wrote "Krvava bajka", the poem about the schoolchildren, during the war, according to the Spomenik Database, which says it was published in 1946 in her book Pesnik i zavičaj. CGTN says she wrote it only days after the killings. The poem imagines a class of children born in the same year, vaccinated against the same diseases and dead on the same day. In Yugoslav schools, children were expected to learn it by heart, the database says. Two films followed: "Prozvan je i V3" in 1962, named after the school class V3, and "Krvava bajka" in 1969.

Planning for a memorial park on the killing ground began in Belgrade in 1953. A competition notice that year said the park should not be a cemetery and not simply a monument to victims, but "primarily" a monument to the heroism and revolutionary spirit of the working class. The winning design, by the landscape architect Smiljan Klaić with the architects Mihajlo Mitrović and Radivoje Tomić, treated the whole landscape as the memorial. Construction began in 1955, and the first monument, "Pain and Defiance" by Ante Gržetić, was unveiled on 21 October 1959.

The centrepiece, "Interrupted Flight" by Miodrag Živković, was opened on 21 October 1963 directly over the mass grave of the executed pupils. It is two white concrete forms rising in a V, which the database reads as a bird with a broken wing and as a reference to the class V3, with faint impressions of children and teachers in its surface. Over several decades more than a dozen monuments were added, including "Circles" by Vojin Bakić, built in 1981 as a gift from Croatia.

The park is still in use. The Spomenik Database says commemorations of the 21 October executions have been held every year since the park opened, and that tens of thousands of people visit annually. CGTN, reporting in August 2025, says a museum nearby keeps handwritten farewells from victims, including a 17-year-old's last note to his parents, and quotes a survivor who remembers the day more than eight decades later.
